topics.headline: Internet-trained models have internet-scale biases; 83% of 388 occupations were more likely followed by a male identifier

source.quote: 83% of the 388 occupations we tested were more likely to be followed by a male identifier by GPT-3.

findings.text: The authors monitored crime and misinformation forums after GPT-2 and found discussion of misuse but no successful deployments; they judged the threat from low- and mid-skill actors as not immediate.

source.quote: we found fewer instances of experimentation and no successful deployments since then.

findings.text: Professional threat analysts told the authors there was no discernible change in advanced persistent threats (APT) operations using language models since GPT-2, in part because steerability was still early.

source.quote: Since the release of GPT-2 there has been no discernible difference in operations that may see potential gains by using language models.

findings.text: Gender co-occurrence completions described women more often with appearance words such as beautiful and gorgeous, while men were described with a wider range of adjectives (Table 6.1).

source.quote: We found females were more often described using appearance oriented words such as ”beautiful” and ”gorgeous” as compared to men

findings.text: When prompted about race, Asian had the highest sentiment in 3 of 7 models and Black the lowest in 5 of 7; gaps narrowed only slightly at larger sizes. Figure 6.1 has no numeric table.

source.quote: Across the models we analyzed, ‘Asian’ had a consistently high sentiment - it ranked 1st in 3 out of 7 models.

findings.text: Completions about Islam favored words such as violent, terrorism, and terrorist more than other religions, and those words were in the top 40 most favored for Islam in GPT-3.

source.quote: words such as violent, terrorism and terrorist co-occurred at a greater rate with Islam than with other religions

findings.text: Humans identified ~200-word GPT-3 175B news articles as machine-written only about 52% of the time (chance is 50%); the paper flags this as relevant to misuse, but the study’s stated aim is generation quality, so those rows are not in evalResults.

source.quote: This task is also relevant to the potential misuse of language models discussed in Section 6.1.

notes: Technical report (Brown et al. 2020), not a system card. Safety content is Section 6 Broader Impacts: qualitative misuse/threat analysis plus gender/race/religion probes. Winogender and occupation-gender rates are the only numeric safety results; Table 6.1 is word co-occurrence counts, Table 6.2 is word lists, Figure 6.1 (racial sentiment) has no readable numbers. Skipped all capability tables (LAMBADA, TriviaQA, SuperGLUE, arithmetic, translation, reading comprehension, NLI, cloze, news-article human detection Tables 3.11–3.12). News detection is cited for misuse but its stated purpose is generation quality. No formal risk-threshold decision. No named external safety tester. interpretability is covered from a one-line limitation, not an interpretability experiment. Training mix percentages in Table 2.2 are not eval scores. Smaller GPT-3 sizes are the paper’s own scaling models, not seed ids.
